summary: This is a clipped excerpt of the IPCC Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C frequently asked questions, covering FAQs 1.1 through 4.1 (partially). It explains why 1.5°C became a target under the Paris Agreement, how close the world is to that warming level, the pathways that could limit warming, the role of energy supply and demand, the impacts of 1.5°C versus 2°C, and the transitions needed. Navigation and figure captions are boilerplate and were largely set aside.
one_line: IPCC FAQ excerpt on the 1.5°C warming target: Paris Agreement origins, current warming, emission pathways, energy, impacts and transitions.
key_facts: The Paris Agreement was adopted by 195 nations at COP21 in December 2015 with the aim of holding warming well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
The Cancun Agreement, adopted at COP16 in 2010, was the first UNFCCC document to mention a 1.5°C limit.
The Structured Expert Dialogue final report concluded that 'in some regions and vulnerable ecosystems, high risks are projected even for warming above 1.5°C'.
The IPCC was invited by the UNFCCC to produce a Special Report in 2018 on the impacts of global warming of 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, known as SR1.5.
The IPCC Special Report uses 1850–1900 as the reference period for pre-industrial temperature.
In the decade 2006–2015, human activity had warmed the world by 0.87°C (±0.12°C) compared to 1850–1900.
Global temperature was rising by 0.2°C (±0.1°C) per decade, so human-induced warming reached about 1°C around 2017 and would reach 1.5°C around 2040 at that pace.
Over a fifth of the global population live in regions that have already experienced warming in at least one season greater than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

The report identifies two main conceptual pathways: one stabilizes global temperature at or just below 1.5°C, and the other, an 'overshoot' pathway, exceeds 1.5°C around mid-century and returns below it before 2100.
Current Nationally Determined Contributions are not on track to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
Net zero CO2 emissions mean the amount of CO2 entering the atmosphere equals the amount removed, which would lead to a near-constant global temperature over many centuries.

Demand-side actions include improving energy efficiency in buildings and reducing consumption of energy- and greenhouse-gas intensive products; supply-side actions include phasing out coal and increasing renewable energy.
Climate change is projected to be a 'poverty multiplier', making the poor poorer and increasing the total number of people living in poverty.
Reaching 2°C instead of 1.5°C would lead to substantial warming of extreme hot days in all land regions and increased heavy rainfall in some regions, particularly high northern latitudes.
Some regions such as the Mediterranean are projected to become drier at 2°C versus 1.5°C of global warming.
Ocean acidification and the persistence of coral reefs are expected to be less damaging in a 1.5°C world than in a 2°C world.
Limiting warming to 1.5°C would require a rapid escalation in the scale and pace of transition, particularly in the next 10–20 years.

entities.name: Paris Agreement
entities.role: 2015 landmark agreement adopted at COP21 that sets the aim of limiting warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels

entities.name: COP21
entities.role: 21st Conference of the Parties in December 2015 where 195 nations adopted the Paris Agreement

entities.name: Cancun Agreement
entities.role: UNFCCC agreement adopted at COP16 in 2010 that first mentioned a 1.5°C limit and established a periodic review of the long-term global goal

entities.name: Structured Expert Dialogue (SED)
entities.role: fact-finding exchange of views between invited experts and UNFCCC delegates during the first review period of the long-term global goal, 2013 to 2015

entities.name: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
entities.role: United Nations body through which countries adopted the Paris Agreement and invited the IPCC to produce SR1.5

entities.name: IPCC
entities.role: body invited by the UNFCCC to provide the Special Report on impacts of 1.5°C of warming and related emission pathways

entities.name: SR1.5
entities.role: IPCC Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C, released in 2018

entities.name: IPCC Fifth Assessment Report
entities.role: earlier IPCC report that used the same 1850–1900 reference period as an approximation of pre-industrial temperatures

entities.name: Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
entities.role: pledges by countries on how they intend to address climate change under the Paris Agreement

entities.name: Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets
entities.role: ice sheets whose collapse on centuries and millennia time scales is given as an example of a tipping point

entities.name: Mediterranean
entities.role: region projected to become drier at 2°C versus 1.5°C of global warming
